bodyHtml:
Which languages are spoken in Western Europe?

October 18, 2021
Languages | Language learning

Planning to reach customers across Western Europe, but unsure which languages you actually need? Europe is packed with languages, and the right choice depends on who you want to speak to.

This overview explains how the main language families fit together, which languages are most widely used in Western Europe, and how that affects your translation project.

In short

  • The EU has 24 official languages, although hundreds more are spoken across Europe.
  • Most European languages descend from Proto-Indo-European and sit in families such as Romance, Germanic, Slavic and Celtic.
  • Spanish, Italian, French, Dutch and Portuguese are among the most widely used Western European languages.
  • Marketing materials and voice-overs need to be accurate and relevant to each target audience.

The EU has 24 official languages.

Source: European Union, EU languages, checked November 2026

Which language families are spoken in Europe?

Europe has fewer official languages than other continents, but the languages it does have are diverse and influential. Many have fascinating roots.

Most European languages still spoken today come from Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of the Indo-European family. That family includes the Romance, Germanic, Armenian, Celtic, Hellenic, Slavic and Baltic languages.

Where these languages first emerged is still debated. Beyond Indo-European, Europe also has the Uralic family and Basque, which is a language isolate with no known relatives.

Romance languages

Romance languages descend from Latin. They include Catalan, Romanian, Spanish, Portuguese, French and Italian.

Germanic languages

English belongs to the Germanic group, alongside German, Dutch, Norwegian, Swedish, Danish, Bavarian and Afrikaans.

It is the world's most widely spoken language once first-language and second-language speakers are counted together.

Around 1.49 billion people worldwide speak English, counting both native and second-language speakers (2026).

Source: Statista Research Department, The most spoken languages worldwide, updated 15 April 2026

If your audience includes German speakers, our German translation services cover business, legal, marketing and technical content.

Slavic languages

The Slavic group includes Slovak, Polish, Czech and Bulgarian, among others. Several are spoken well beyond their home countries, especially Russian.

Baltic languages

The living Baltic languages are Lithuanian and Latvian. The group also includes extinct languages such as Old Prussian and Selonian.

Celtic languages

Celtic languages fall into two branches. Welsh, Cornish and Breton are Brittonic, while Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx are Goidelic.

Despite their age, some are still in everyday use. Welsh is a clear example, as the 2021 census shows.

An estimated 538,000 usual residents of Wales aged three and over (17.8%) could speak Welsh in 2021, down from 562,000 (19.0%) in 2011.

Source: Office for National Statistics, Welsh language, Wales: Census 2021

Hellenic languages

Greek is the main living language of the Hellenic branch of Indo-European.

Albanian

Albanian forms a branch of Indo-European on its own.

Armenian

Armenian is spoken by most people living in Armenia, as well as by communities in Russia and Iran.

Europe's two other language groups are Uralic and Basque. Uralic includes the Finnic and Ugric languages, while Basque is spoken in parts of northern Spain and south-western France.

Which languages are most widely used in Western Europe?

Western European languages are mostly Romance languages from south-western and central Europe, plus Germanic languages from northern Europe, the British Isles and central Europe.

Languages usually counted in the region include:

  • Irish
  • Scots
  • Scottish Gaelic
  • Manx
  • Welsh
  • Breton
  • Cornish
  • Basque
  • Maltese
  • French
  • Portuguese
  • Italian
  • Spanish
  • Dutch

Among the most widely used are Spanish, Italian, French, Dutch and Portuguese. You may have studied one of them at school, or considered learning one before a trip to travel around Western Europe.

Here is a closer look at each.

Spanish

Spanish is the most widely spoken Romance language, and Spain is only part of the picture. Most native speakers live in the Americas.

The Spanish native-speaker community passed 500 million for the first time in 2025, reaching 520 million. Counting all potential speakers, including those with limited competence, the total is 635,743,644.

Source: Instituto Cervantes, El español en el mundo 2025 (the 520 million figure is native speakers, L1; the total includes limited-competence speakers)

Like the other Romance languages, Spanish descends from Latin. The standard form we see in writing today is based on Castilian.

The Royal Spanish Academy, founded in Madrid in 1713, helps standardise the language and maintains its reference dictionaries.

Italian

Italian is spoken in Italy, Switzerland, San Marino and Vatican City. It comes from Latin and developed over a long period after the Roman Empire fell in the 5th century.

Italian documents survive from as far back as 960 CE, with the first real flowering of writing at the start of the 13th century. Modern Italian is built on the Tuscan dialect, with many other influences.

French

French is a Romance language that is an official language in many countries across several continents, not only France.

Its roots lie in Gaul, the Roman province that covered much of modern France. The Gaulish language left only a small mark, but a number of its words passed into Latin and from there into French.

Its Latin roots are one reason many English speakers find French easier to learn than some other languages. The same is true of other Romance languages.

Dutch

Dutch is the language of the Netherlands and Flanders, and it is an official language in Aruba, Curaçao and St Maarten.

Dutch is the mother tongue of more than 25 million people.

Source: Nederlandse Taalunie, About the Taalunie (native-speaker figure, L1)

Dutch developed from Old Franconian in medieval times. Old Dutch became Middle Dutch, which then split into various dialects.

The language was standardised in the 17th century, partly through the Dutch edition of the Bible produced under the Dutch Republic. You can read more about our Dutch translation work.

Portuguese

Portuguese is spoken in Portugal and across the world, with Brazil home to most speakers.

It began on the western Iberian Peninsula as Latin, introduced by the Romans. After the Roman Empire collapsed, Latin developed there into Galician-Portuguese.

Galician and Portuguese then gradually separated, and Portuguese developed into the language we know today.
